If you do buy into something new, buy the smallest amount the platform allows, sell a portion immediately, and only then consider a real position.

sections.heading: The Only Defence That Always Works
sections.body: Size your position so that being wrong does not matter. Every check above reduces risk; none eliminates it. The people who survive rug pulls are the ones who treat any young token as money already spent.

articles.title: What Is a Hardware Wallet and Do You Need One?
articles.description: A hardware wallet keeps your private key offline and physically confirms each transaction. Here is what it protects against, and what it does not.
articles.author: CryptoNav Team

toc.title: What It Does Not Protect Against

sections.heading: The Idea in One Paragraph
sections.body:
A hardware wallet is a small device that stores your private key and signs transactions only after you physically confirm them. The key never touches your computer or phone, so malware on those devices has nothing to steal.

That is the whole design. Everything else — the screen, the buttons, the companion app — exists to make that one property usable.

sections.heading: What It Protects Against
sections.body:
- **Malware reading your key.** The key is not in a file on a machine that has internet access.
- **Signing the wrong thing.** A malicious site cannot drain you without you approving on the device itself, where it shows the real recipient and amount.
- **Compromised computer.** Even a fully infected machine cannot move funds it cannot sign for.
- **Exchange failure.** You are the counterparty to no company.

sections.heading: What It Does Not Protect Against
sections.body:
A hardware wallet is not a magic shield, and understanding the gaps matters more than the feature list:

- **You approving a bad transaction.** If you confirm it, it is authorised. Read the device screen.
- **Your seed phrase being stolen.** The device is replaceable; the words are not. If someone photographs your backup, the hardware is irrelevant.
- **Phishing that imitates the device flow.** Some attacks convince you to type your phrase into a fake "recovery" page.
- **Supplier tampering.** Buy directly from the manufacturer, never a marketplace reseller.

sections.heading: How Setup Works
sections.body:
You receive a device and generate a new seed phrase on it. Write the words down by hand, in order, and store them offline. Verify the backup by restoring it once before you fund it — discovering a bad backup while holding a balance is the worst way to learn.

Set a PIN. If the device offers a passphrase, understand that it creates a hidden wallet, and losing the passphrase loses that wallet permanently.

sections.heading: Who Actually Needs One
sections.body:
If the total you hold would genuinely hurt to lose, a hardware wallet is the cheapest insurance available, at a fraction of a percent of what it protects.

If you are holding a small amount you actively trade, a well-reviewed hot wallet plus disciplined approval hygiene is a reasonable choice. Most people settle on both: hot for spending, hardware for savings.

sections.heading: Choosing One
sections.body: Prioritise a long track record, open or independently audited firmware, a secure element chip, and a screen and buttons on the device itself so you can verify what you are signing. Our wallet directory compares cold storage options on exactly those attributes.

articles.title: What Are Gas Fees? Why Crypto Transactions Cost Money
articles.description: Gas fees pay the network to process your transaction. Learn why they rise, how they are calculated, and how to pay less without waiting forever.
articles.author: CryptoNav Team

sections.heading: What Gas Actually Is
sections.body:
Gas is a unit of computational work. Every operation a transaction performs costs a fixed amount of gas, and you pay that gas at a price set by the market.

Your fee is gas used multiplied by gas price. A simple transfer uses far less than a complex swap, which is why two transactions in the same block can cost wildly different amounts.

sections.heading: Why Fees Swing So Far
sections.body:
Block space is limited. When more transactions want into a block than fit, the price of inclusion rises until enough drop out. That is the entire mechanism.

Practical consequences:

- Congestion events — a popular mint or a market crash — push fees to absurd levels within minutes.
- Quiet weekends are cheap.
- Fees are usually quoted in the chain's own token, so a spike in that token's price raises the dollar cost of the same work.

sections.heading: The Two-Part Fee on Ethereum
sections.body:
Ethereum splits the fee into a base fee and a priority fee:

- **Base fee** is set by the protocol from how full the last block was. It is burned — destroyed — rather than paid to anyone.
- **Priority fee** (a tip) is what you offer validators to include you sooner.

You set a maximum you are willing to pay. If the base fee rises above it, your transaction waits. This is why a transaction can sit pending for hours during a spike.

sections.heading: How to Pay Less
sections.body:
- **Wait.** Fees are cyclical. Off-peak windows are common; a pending transaction can be cheaper to resubmit later than to push through now.
- **Use a Layer 2.** Rollups settle to Ethereum while charging a fraction of the fee. For everyday use this is the single biggest saving.
- **Check before you act.** Fee estimators show current conditions. A dapp that never displays them is hiding the cost.
- **Do not over-tip in a quiet market.** When blocks are half empty, the minimum works.
- **Batch when you can.** One well-constructed transaction beats several small ones.

sections.heading: If a Transaction Is Stuck
sections.body:
A pending transaction occupies your nonce, so later ones queue behind it. You can either wait, or send a replacement with the same nonce and a higher fee. Cancelling means replacing with a zero-value self-transfer at a higher fee — you pay to undo it.

On most modern wallets this is a single "speed up" button. Understanding what it does prevents surprises.

articles.title: How to Track a Crypto Portfolio Across Wallets and Chains
articles.description: Manual spreadsheets break as soon as you use a second chain. Here is how portfolio trackers work, what to look for, and how to keep records clean.
articles.author: CryptoNav Team

sections.heading: Why Tracking Gets Hard Fast
sections.body:
A single-exchange portfolio is easy to track: the exchange shows you a number. The moment you hold assets in a self-custody wallet, or use a second chain, the number becomes a research project.

Add staking rewards, an airdrop, a bridge between two chains, and a swap that is also a taxable event, and a spreadsheet built by hand stops being trustworthy within weeks.

sections.heading: Two Approaches
sections.body:
**Read-only wallet tracking.** You give the tracker your public addresses (never a private key) and it reads balances and history directly from the chain. Nothing is deposited anywhere, and it works for any wallet you control.

**Exchange integration.** You connect an API key with read-only permissions, and the tracker imports your trade history. Useful for cost-basis records, and only safe with trading and withdrawal permissions switched off.

sections.heading: What to Look For
sections.body:
- **Chain coverage.** Trackers are only as useful as the chains they read. Check yours specifically.
- **Read-only or nothing.** Any tool asking for a private key or seed phrase is not a tracker.
- **Cost-basis support.** The method your jurisdiction requires should be available.
- **Historical imports.** A tracker that only sees the present cannot reconstruct a past gain.
- **Export.** You need to be able to get your data out, in a format an accountant can read.

sections.heading: Habits That Keep Records Clean
sections.body:
- Use one address per purpose — savings, trading, experiments — so history stays legible.
- Label transfers between your own wallets immediately, while you still remember them.
- Export history from every exchange at least annually. Exchanges close, and a closed exchange is a missing cost basis.
- Reconcile monthly, not at tax time. Small corrections are cheap; a year of them is not.
- Keep the raw exports even after importing. The tracker is a view, not the record.

sections.heading: Where to Start
sections.body: Our utilities directory compares portfolio trackers and tax calculators on chains supported, features and cost. Start with one that covers the chains you actually use rather than the one with the longest feature list.

articles.title: What Is a Crypto Exchange? CEX vs DEX Explained
articles.description: Centralised and decentralised exchanges solve the same problem differently. Understand the trade-offs in custody, fees and control before you pick.
articles.author: CryptoNav Team

sections.heading: What an Exchange Does
sections.body: An exchange matches buyers with sellers and sets a price. Beyond that simple job, the two families of exchange diverge sharply — and the difference determines who holds your coins.

sections.heading: Centralised Exchanges (CEX)
sections.body:
A centralised exchange is a company that runs the order book. You create an account, verify your identity, deposit funds, and the exchange holds them on your behalf.

**Advantages:**
- Fiat on-ramp — the easiest way to turn a bank transfer into crypto.
- Deep liquidity, fast execution, and familiar order types.
- Customer support and, in regulated jurisdictions, a complaints process.

**Costs:**
- You do not hold your keys. Withdrawals can be frozen, and exchange failures have lost customer funds before.
- Identity verification is mandatory in most countries.
- Trading fees plus spread, and withdrawal fees on top.

sections.heading: Decentralised Exchanges (DEX)
sections.body:
A DEX is a set of smart contracts. You connect a wallet and trade directly from it, and every trade settles on-chain.

**Advantages:**
- Self-custody throughout — you never hand over your coins.
- No account, no identity check, no permission needed.
- Censorship-resistant: no company can freeze your access.

**Costs:**
- You pay the network fee on every trade, which on a busy chain can exceed the trade value.
- Liquidity is fragmented and slippage is real on thin pairs.
- No one to call if something goes wrong. A mistaken swap is final.
- Interacting with contracts exposes you to contract risk.

sections.heading: Choosing Between Them
sections.body:
Most people use both, for different jobs:

- Buying with a bank transfer, or selling a large position: a centralised exchange, for liquidity and a fiat ramp.
- Swapping tokens without an account, or trading a long tail: a DEX.
- Holding long-term: neither. Move savings to self-custody.

The mistake is treating an exchange balance as a wallet. It is a position at a company, and it carries that company's risk.

sections.heading: What to Check Before Depositing
sections.body:
For a CEX: is it licensed where you live, how long has it operated, and does it publish proof of reserves? Search its name with "withdrawal delay" first — deposits are always fast and withdrawals are where problems appear.

For a DEX: how much liquidity is in the pool you intend to use, and has the protocol been audited and live long enough to have a track record?

Our exchange directory lists centralised and decentralised venues side by side with fees, chains and safety records.

articles.title: How to Use a Crypto Wallet Safely: A Practical Guide
articles.description: Sending, receiving, approvals and backups — the day-to-day habits that prevent the most common ways people lose crypto.
articles.author: CryptoNav Team
articles.keyword: how to use a crypto wallet

toc.title: The Two Things a Wallet Does
Backups: The Part You Cannot Fix Later

sections.heading: The Two Things a Wallet Does
sections.body:
A wallet does not store coins. The coins exist on the blockchain; the wallet holds the key that proves they are yours, and signs transactions that move them.

That reframing explains almost every security rule below: the goal is never to expose the key, and never to sign something you did not mean.

sections.heading: Receiving: Addresses and Networks
sections.body:
Every wallet has an address per network. Two rules prevent most lost funds:

1. **Match the network.** Sending an Ethereum-network token to a Solana address is usually unrecoverable. Check the network on both sides.
2. **Send a test amount first.** A small transfer costs little and proves the path works before the real one.

Some chains also need a memo or tag when sending to an exchange. Omitting it can strand the deposit in the exchange's shared wallet.

sections.heading: Sending: Verify Before You Sign
sections.body:
Before confirming any transfer:

- Paste the address; never retype it. Clipboard-hijacking malware exists and swaps addresses at paste time.
- Check the first and last characters against the source, not just the middle.
- Confirm the network and the fee.
- Send a small test when the destination is new.

If a wallet popup shows a different amount or address than you intended, reject it and start over.

sections.heading: Approvals: The Most Ignored Risk
sections.body:
When a dapp asks to "spend" your tokens, you are granting a contract permission — often an unlimited amount, forever. Those approvals persist after you close the tab.

- Approve the specific amount you need, not unlimited, when the interface allows it.
- Review and revoke approvals periodically. Most wallets and several free services show what you have granted and let you cancel.
- An unlimited approval to a contract that later turns malicious is a standing drain on that token.

sections.heading: Backups: The Part You Cannot Fix Later
sections.body:
- Write the seed phrase by hand, in order, offline.
- Never photograph it, never store it in cloud notes or a chat draft.
- Never type it into any website. Every request for it is theft.
- Store it where a fire cannot reach it and a house guest cannot find it.
- Consider splitting storage across two locations so no single accident destroys it.

sections.heading: A Simple Routine That Works
sections.body:
Daily: use a hot wallet with a small balance for interactions, and read every confirmation. Monthly: revoke approvals you no longer need and reconcile what you hold. Yearly: export exchange history and verify a backup restore on a spare device.

None of this is exotic. It is the difference between losing funds to a mistake you could have prevented and not.
